label: Title
notes: Open by reframing Ricci curvature as an operator on metrics rather than as a static tensor. The chapter asks what can be prescribed locally, which compatibility equations are unavoidable, and how analytic or elliptic structure changes the problem from tensor algebra into PDE.

label: PDE Viewpoint
notes: Use this slide to establish the central translation. The unknown is not a function but a positive definite matrix of functions. The equation is second order and nonlinear, but a large part of the difficulty comes from coordinates: pulling a solution back by a diffeomorphism is still a solution in transformed data.

label: Ricci Operator
notes: The formula is intentionally schematic. It prevents a common misunderstanding: Ricci is not simply a Laplacian of the metric. Its highest derivative part has a Laplace-like core only after choosing a useful gauge, while the inverse metric and first derivative products keep the equation nonlinear.

label: Gauge Degeneracy
notes: Stress that gauge is not a nuisance added by analysts; it is forced by geometry. The same metric up to pullback gives the same curvature content, so the raw differential operator cannot behave like an elliptic system on every component until this redundancy is controlled.

label: Pointwise Solvability
notes: The important distinction is between prescribing Ricci at a point and prescribing it on an open set. At a point, after choosing normal coordinates, enough second jet freedom remains to hit many targets. On an open set, derivatives of the target and compatibility identities begin to matter.

label: Bianchi Compatibility
notes: Present Bianchi as a conservation law for curvature. It is not an extra theorem one checks after solving; it is a necessary compatibility condition any target tensor must survive. This also explains why prescribed Ricci curvature is subtler than prescribing a random symmetric matrix field.

label: Gauge Fixing
notes: This is the analytical turning point. The slide should not be sold as magic: the Laplacian form is a leading-order statement, not the whole equation. The point is that once a slice is chosen, standard elliptic intuition becomes relevant.

label: Local Einstein Construction
notes: Describe this as a local germ construction. Students should hear the difference between prescribing enough analytic Cauchy data and solving a complete global boundary value problem. The visual slice emphasizes that the solution is grown near a hypersurface.

label: Regularity Ladder
notes: Connect this to the appendix material on elliptic operators without assuming the audience has all estimates memorized. The local message is that the PDE does not merely test existing smooth metrics; under suitable hypotheses it can force improved regularity.

label: Analyticity
notes: The phrase suitable coordinates is doing real work. Analyticity is not a coordinate-free claim about arbitrary smooth charts; it is obtained after placing the metric in coordinates where the Einstein equation becomes an analytic elliptic system.

label: Uniqueness
notes: This slide should temper the previous existence discussion. A construction theorem and a uniqueness theorem are not opposites; they ask different things. Emphasize that coordinate freedom must be fixed before comparing two local metrics component by component.

label: Nonexistence
notes: Make nonexistence concrete. A proposed right-hand side may look harmless as a symmetric tensor field, yet fail a necessary identity once one asks for it to be Ricci of some metric. This is a PDE obstruction, not just a topological obstruction.

label: Conformal Model
notes: Use the conformal model as a sanity check. In two dimensions, Ricci contains no more information than Gaussian curvature, so the equation collapses to a scalar equation. That makes the second-order nature and the role of coordinates immediately visible.

label: PDE Anatomy Table
notes: This table is the lecture’s organizing memory. Ask students to place each theorem or construction from the chapter into one row. The table also helps prevent overgeneralization: a pointwise algebraic statement does not automatically imply a local analytic one.

label: Learner Lab
notes: Use this slide as a structured checkpoint rather than as extra homework. The first prompt asks students to connect a sign computation to geometric curvature in the conformal model. The second prompt makes them test a proposed Ricci target before trying to solve for a metric, which reinforces the role of compatibility identities. The third prompt returns to gauge: two formulas may describe the same local geometry after a diffeomorphism, so comparison requires a chosen normalization. Ask for compact explanations that name the first obstruction or freedom they detect.

label: Recap
notes: Close by tying the chapter back to the course arc. Earlier chapters built curvature and variational language; this one teaches how local Einstein geometry is constrained by the analytic behavior of the Ricci operator. The key takeaway is that geometric freedom and PDE rigidity coexist.
